enhancement of pharmaceutical removal and microbial community change 
of the novel anaerobic baffled biofilm - membrane bioreactor in treating 
building wastewater

A B S T R A C T   
This research aims to conduct a comparative investigation of the role played by microaeration and sludge 
recirculation in the novel anaerobic baffled biofilm-membrane bioreactor (AnBB-MBR) for enhancing pharma­
ceutical removal from building wastewater. Three AnBB-MBRs — R1: AnBB-MBR, R2: AnBB-MBR with 
microaeration and R3: AnBB-MBR with microaeration and sludge recirculation — were operated simultaneously 
to remove Ciprofloxacin (CIP), Caffeine (CAF), Sulfamethoxazole (SMX) and Diclofenac (DCF) from real building 
wastewater at the hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 30 h for 115 days. From the removal profiles of the targeted 
pharmaceuticals in the AnBB-MBRs, it was found that the fixed-film compartment (C1) could significantly reduce 
the targeted pharmaceuticals. The remaining pharmaceuticals were further removed with the microaeration 
compartment. R2 exhibited the utmost removal efficiency for CIP (78.0 %) and DCF (40.8 %), while SMX was 
removed most successfully by R3 (microaeration with sludge recirculation) at 91.3 %, followed by microaeration 
in R2 (88.5 %). For CAF, it was easily removed by all AnBB-MBR systems (>90 %). The removal mechanisms 
indicate that the microaeration in R2 facilitated the adsorption of CIP onto microaerobic biomass, while the 
enhanced biodegradation of CAF, SMX and DCF was confirmed by batch biotransformation kinetics and the 
adsorption isotherms of the targeted pharmaceuticals. The microbial groups involved in biodegradation of the

1. Introduction 
Recently, pharmaceuticals have been detected in the effluent from 
wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) in the range of ng/L to μg/L as a 
result of WWTPs not being designed to remove these pharmaceuticals 
efficiently (Tran et al., 2018). The contamination of the water envi­
ronment by pharmaceuticals could pose an ecological risk to aquatic and 
terrestrial environments in the short and/or long-term, such as from the 
occurrence of antibiotic resistant genes, reproductive problems, cyto­
logical alterations, and lethality. Moreover, human health can also be 
negatively impacted by the accumulation of pharmaceuticals in the food 
chain, particularly through the water consumed for agricultural and 
livestock farming (Fent et al., 2006). 
Ciprofloxacin (CIP), Caffeine (CAF), Sulfamethoxazole (SMX) and 
Diclofenac (DCF) are the main pharmaceuticals commonly found in 
surface water and effluents of WWTPs in Thailand with a high hazard 
quotient remaining in the water basin reported by various studies 
(Sinthuchai et al., 2021; Tewari et al., 2013). CAF is a psychostimulant 
and analeptic drug used to alleviate drowsiness and lethargy (Frederic 
and Yves, 2014). CIP is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that has an impact 
on aquatic organisms at concentrations in the range of a few hundred 
μg/L (Nguyen et al., 2019), and SMX is an oral sulfonamide antibiotic 
used for the treatment of various bacterial infections (Xu et al., 2022). 
DCF is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), whose acute 
and chronic toxicity to aquatic organisms has been reported at a level of 
one to a hundred μg/L (Triebskorn et al., 2004). 
Recently, anaerobic treatment has been widely incorporated into 
membrane bioreactor (MBR) to create the anaerobic membrane biore­
actor (AnMBR), which has many benefits including in terms of total 
microbial sludge retention, high effluent quality, and high toxic waste­
water tolerance. Most previous studies in the fields of pharmaceutical 
removal by anaerobic MBR have focused on completely stirred tank 
reactor (CSTR), upflow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB), fluidized, 
submerged anaerobic MBR, etc. (Ji et al., 2020; Oberoi et al., 2022). 
Buakaew and Ratanatamskul (2021) developed inclined-tubes to be 
used in the fixed film system that offers high retention of the microbial 
sludges and promotes biofilm growth inside the combined AnBB-MBR, 
which could efficiently remove organics and nutrients from building 
wastewater, and the system could operate at a stable flux for long 
experimental runs. Furthermore, this system exhibits high biomass 
retention capabilities, which could accommodate many types of mi­
croorganisms, based on the abundance of baffled compartments that was 
supposed to be an efficient wastewater treatment system (Ratana­
tamskul and Katasomboon, 2017). In addition, the biofilm layer was 
reported as being able to prevent the toxic effects caused to microbes by 
toxic compounds, and to enhance the biodegradation of many pollutants 
(Carneiro et al., 2019). 
It has been reported that microaeration with low amounts of oxygen 
up to 1 LO2/Lfeed and dissolved oxygen (DO) in the range of 0.1–1 mg/L 
is able to enhance the removal of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and nitrogen 
in the anaerobic treatment process (Buakaew and Ratanatamskul, 
2023). In addition, a low amount of oxygen has also been found to play a 
role in influencing the redox equilibrium of NADH/NAD+, thereby 
stimulating the production of enzymes by acidogenic biomass and 
enhancing the rate of hydrolysis (Huili˜nir et al., 2023). Another study 
reported that pharmaceutical removal in the anaerobic UASB system 
with a short HRT of 7.4 h, using microaeration equivalent to 
0.025–0.152 L.O2/Lfeed could also improve SMX and DCF removal (do 
Nascimento et al., 2021). 
Furthermore, sludge recirculation has been commonly utilized in 
anoxic/oxic bioreactors (A/O) to mitigate the accumulation of nitrate 
(NO3
−) for enhancing the effectiveness of nitrogen removal from building 
wastewater (Fathali et al., 2019). The sludge recirculation might also 
enhance the biodegradation of slowly biodegradable organic matters in 
the wastewater due to variations in the environment conditions (anoxic/ 
oxic conditions). At present, there is little information on the effect of 
sludge recirculation on pharmaceutical removal in the microaerobic/ 
anoxic biotreatment systems. Therefore, there is a need for research to 
investigate the effect of sludge recirculation in the microaerobic/anoxic 
compartments of AnBB-MBR in order to determine the possible impact 
on the removal of pharmaceuticals as well as on the membrane fouling 
of the system in treating domestic building wastewater contaminated 
with pharmaceuticals. 
This work aims to develop novel microaerobic AnBB-MBR systems 
with microaeration at 0.1 L/min (0.93 LO2/LFeed) with and without 
sludge recirculation for enhancing the removal of the targeted phar­
maceuticals (CIP, CAF, SMX and DCF) in the AnBB-MBR. At present, no 
research has focused on the removal of pharmaceuticals by this pro­
posed system. In addition, the effectiveness of microaeration in the 
anaerobic process of AnBB-MBR should be more clearly understood in 
terms of how microaeration affects the pharmaceutical removal mech­
anisms, the fate, biotransformation rate, and adsorption, as compared to 
anaerobic AnBB-MBR. Here, the AnBB-MBR systems were developed for 
three distinct bioreactors — an AnBB-MBR system (without micro­
aeraton), an AnBB-MBR with microaeration, and an AnBB-MBR system 
incorporating microaeration and sludge recirculation — in order to gain 
insights into how a low airflow (0.1 L/min) and sludge recirculation 
could affect the pharmaceutical fate and removal. At present, no 
comparative study has been conducted on the effects of microaeration 
and microaeration plus sludge recirculation in AnBB-MBR on enhancing 
pharmaceuticals. Also, the comparative study of biotransformation ki­
netic rates and adsorption of the targeted compounds between micro­
aerobic and anaerobic AnBB-MBR intensively investigated the different 
behaviors of anaerobic and microaerobic biomasses (biofilms and sus­
pended sludges) on pharmaceutical removal in two batch experiments 
for active and inactive biomasses. This work also examined the organic 
removal performances of the systems, specifically focusing on parame­
ters such as VFAs, and dissolved methane organic constituents. Addi­
tionally, the biomass characteristics, membrane fouling tendencies, and 
microbial community structure of the three AnBB-MBR systems were 
investigated in order to gain a comprehensive understanding of the 
system performance. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Three AnBB-MBR configurations 
As shown in Fig. 1, three AnBB-MBRs were constructed with iden­
tical dimensions of 60 cm in height, 45 cm in length, and 15 cm in width. 
Each system was divided into three compartments using baffles. The 
volume ratios of the first compartment (C1), second compartment (C2), 
and third compartment (C3) were 11.25 L, 11.25 L, and 18 L, respec­
tively. Both C1 and C2 were filled with two sets of fixed films made of 
fiber glass filter (Glass filter mat, AQUA-NEAT, Japan). These filter sets 
had a specific area of 500 m2.m−3 and a total volume of 4.5 L to capture 
and retain the biomass by promoting the growth of biofilm.

Furthermore, C3 of the three bioreactors were filled with moving bed 
(MVB) media at a volume ratio of 30 % (Vmedia:Vcompartment). The 
MVB media was made of polyethylene with a circular length of 2.5 cm, a 
thickness of 0.11 cm and an active surface area of 4850 m2.m−3. The 
proposes of this MVB were to promote biofilm growth, facilitate mem­
brane scouring and provide mixing in the C3 zone by using a sonic pump 
(AP1600). Each C3 of the three bioreactors contained a ceramic flat 
sheet microfiltration membrane (Ceraflo, Singapore) with a pore size of 
0.5 μm and an average surface area of 0.107 m2. A vacuum pressure 
gauge was connected to the membrane to monitor the transmembrane 
pressure (TMP). Feeding, permeates and sludge recirculation were 
operated by metering pumps (Prominent, Germany). Level sensors were 
applied to control the wastewater level inside the bioreactors. In this 
study, the first bioreactor was a control reactor of anaerobic baffled 
biofilm-MBR (R1: AnBB-MBR). The second bioreactor was the AnBB- 
MBR with microaeration (R2: AnBB-MBR with microaeration) using 
an air flowrate of 0.1 Lair/min in C3 by controlling the DO using a DO 
controller (Ponpe Instruments, Thailand) corresponding to DO in the 
range of 0.3–0.7 mg/L and oxygen supply rate at 0.93 LO2/Lfeed. The 
third bioreactor was the AnBB-MBR with the same microaeration as the 
second bioreactor, and sludge recirculation at 200 % was conducted 
from C3 to C2 (R3: AnBB-MBR with microaeration and sludge recircu­
lation) to promote the anoxic/microaerobic conditions. This anoxic 
condition might enhance the biodegradation of SMX (Li et al., 2023b). 
The measured DO concentrations in C3 throughout the experimental 
runs were in the range of 0–0.2 mg/L, 0.3–0.7 mg/L and 0.3–0.7 mg/L 
for R1, R2 and R3, respectively (Supplementary data Fig. S1).

Mahitaladhibesra Building, Chulalongkorn University was used as the

consisted of chemical COD 245.80 ± 94.18 mg/L, TKN 88.43 ± 6.4 mg/

purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (USA) were separately prepared in an 
individual stock solution at 2 g/L and kept at −20 ◦C before spiking. The 
CIP was prepared in 0.1 % formic acid solution; The CAF was prepared in 
Milli-Q water and the SMX and DCF were prepared in pure methanol. 
For the experimental runs of the three bioreactors, all targeted com­
pounds were continuously spiked in the influent tank (750 l) until they 
reached 250 μg/L since this value is higher than the concentration of 
pharmaceuticals detected in the influent of WWTPs globally (Tran et al., 
2018). The anaerobic sludges from a textile WWTP that were filled into 
C1 and C2 of the three bioreactors at 30 % of reactor volume were 
continuously acclimated with high-rise building wastewater with the 
targeted pharmaceuticals over three months before starting the experi­
mental run. 
The three bioreactors were then simultaneously operated in experi­
mental runs for 115 d at a solid retention time (SRT) 100 d (calculated 
from C3 compartment) and constant HRT of 30 h (optimal value from 
the previous pilot-scale testing), which was divided into an HRT of 8.33 
h in each C1 and C2 and 13.33 h in C3 of the AnBB-MBRs. The permeate 
flow rate was controlled in an intermittent manner. Specifically, it 
involved 8 min of suction followed by 2 min of relaxation to avoid 
excessive membrane stress. The permeate fluxes of the three bioreactors 
were kept constant at 12.6 L.m−2.h−1 to evaluate the fouling rate by 
TMP evaluation. After the TMP reached 375 mmHg, the membranes 
were removed from the reactors for cleaning. The cleaning process 
involved scrubbing the fouling substances on the membrane surfaces 
and then immersing them in a solution of 0.4 % NaOCl for 8 h. Subse­
quently, the membranes were washed with tap water and soaked in 0.4 
% nitric acid for another 8 h. Finally, they were rinsed again with tap 
water before being reused in the AnBB-MBRs. 
2.3. Analytical methods 
COD, mixed liquor suspended solids (MLSS) and mixed liquor vola­
tile suspended solids (MLVSS) were analyzed using standard methods 
(APHA, 2017). To determine the biomass concentration of the biofilms 
on the MVBs, ten MVBs from C3 of each bioreactor were dried overnight 
at 60 ◦C, followed by weighing. To detach the biofilms from the MVBs, a 
series of washing steps were performed. Firstly, the dried biofilms were 
washed and scrubbed with 6 % NaOCl solution, followed by 0.4 % HNO3 
and then deionized water. Subsequently, the MVBs were once again 
dried overnight at 60 ◦C, and their weights were measured to determine 
the weight of the fresh MVBs in order to obtain the attached biofilms 
weights. The pH and ORP of the wastewater were analyzed using a pH/ 
ORP meter - HI 98121 (Hanna instruments, Italy). The zeta potential of 
the biomass in C3 was measured using a Zetasizer Nano ZSP (Malvern, 
England). A particle size distribution of the sludges in C3 of each 
bioreactor was performed using a laser particle size distribution 
analyzer - Mastersizer 3000 (Malvern, England). 
The surface morphology of the fresh and used MVBs were visualized 
using a Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) JSM-IT500HR, JED-2300 
(JEOL, USA). To extract soluble microbial products (SMP) and loosely 
and tightly bound extracellular polymeric substances (L-EPS and T-EPS) 
from the suspended sludges and the foulants on the membrane, the 
suspended sludge samples were analyzed for MLSS and then 25 mL were 
added into the centrifuge tubes while the foulants were weighed and 
subsequently 25 mL of deionized (DI) water was added and mixed 
vigorously. After mixing and vortexing for 1 min, the samples were 
centrifuged at 4000g for 10 mins resulting in the separation of the su­
pernatants containing SMP. Next, the dewatered sludges were mixed 
with 25 mL of a 0.9 % NaCl solution, vortexed, and centrifuged again. 
The supernatants obtained from this step represented L-EPS. Lastly, the 
remaining dewatered sludges were resuspended in another 25 mL of a 
0.9 % NaCl solution and incubated in a water bath at 60 ◦C for 1 h 
followed by vortexing and centrifuging again; the supernatants in this 
case were representative of T-EPS. The modified phenol‑sulfuric acid 
method was employed to determine the carbohydrate content using 
glucose as a standard (BeMiller, 2017), and the modified Lowry method, 
with bovine albumin serum as a standard was used to assess the protein 
content (Markwell et al., 1978). The three dimensions of the fluores­
cence excitation-emission matrix (3D-FEEM) spectra of the influent and 
mix liquors in C3 in each bioreactor were examined by measuring the 
excitation (Ex) spectra between 200 and 550 nm and the emission (Em) 
spectra between 250 and 550 nm. The samples were filtered through a 
0.45 μm filter, and a fluorescence spectrofluorometer (Aqualog®, 
HORIBA Scientific., USA) was used to analyze them with an integration 
time of the excitation wavelength of 3 min. SCD1 served as the detector, 
with a grating density of 1200 for excitation and 285 for emission 
wavelengths. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) — con­
ducted using a Perkin Elmer Spectrum: One instrument with a wave­
length range of 4000 to 400 cm−1 — was employed to examine the 
functional groups present in the organic membrane foulants. Prior to the 
FTIR analysis, the foulants were subjected to drying at 60 ◦C for 8 h to 
obtain dried samples for analysis. 
Analysis of VFAs, including acetic acid, propionic acid, butyric acid, 
isobutyric acid, butyric acid, and isovaleric acid, was carried out using 
gas chromatography with a flame ionization detector (GC-FID) with a 
DB-WAX column (30 m × 0.25 mm, Agilent, USA). Calibration curves 
for all measurements were prepared using VFA standards (35,272, 
Restek) with concentrations ranging from 2 to 200 mg/L. The column 
was set at 90 ◦C, and the temperature was increased at a rate of 4 ◦C/min 
until it reached 140 ◦C. Subsequently, the temperature was increased at 
a rate of 25 ◦C/min up to 250 ◦C, and this temperature was maintained 
for 2 mins. The injector and detector temperatures were both set at 
250 ◦C. Helium gas (99.99 %, Praxair, Canada) was used as the carrier 
gas at a pressure of 97.6 kPa. Prior to analysis, all samples underwent 
acidification with ortho-phosphoric acid to achieve a pH of 2–3. After 
acidification, the samples were centrifuged at 4500 rpm for 10 min, and 
the resulting supernatants were filtered using a nylon syringe filter 
(0.22 μm) before being injected into the GC system. Dissolved methane 
analysis in the permeate of each bioreactor was carried out using the 
headspace method modified by DelSontro et al. (2016). A 500 mL sy­
ringe was connected to a stopcock valve to collect 250 mL of the 
permeated tube followed by the injection of 250 mL of nitrogen gas into 
the headspace, after which, the stopcock valve was closed immediately. 
The syringe was then shaken for 5 min to allow for equilibrium between 
the liquid and gas phases based on Henry’s law. The gas in the headspace 
was analyzed using a GC equipped with a thermal conductivity detector 
(GC-TCD). The dissolved methane concentration was determined using 
Eq. (1):

2.4. Analysis of targeted pharmaceuticals 
For the extraction of targeted pharmaceuticals in the liquid phase, 5 
mL of the samples were first filtered by nylon syringe filter 0.45 μm to 
eliminate suspended solids and then diluted to 100 mL with Milli-Q 
water. Solid-phase extraction (SPE) was performed using 6 mL, 200 
mg Oasis HLB cartridges (Waters, Milford, MA, USA) equipped with a

vacuum manifold pump. The cartridges were initially conditioned with 
5 mL methanol followed by 5 mL Milli-Q water, and the samples were 
immediately loaded at the flowrate of 2–3 drops/s. The cartridges were 
then washed with 5 mL of Milli-Q water and vacuum dried for 30 min. 
Next, the analytes were gently eluted with 5 mL of methanol. Subse­
quently, the eluents were dried with a gentle stream of nitrogen until 
they were close to dryness, after which they were reconstituted in 5 mL 
of 50 % methanol in Milli-Q water. Finally, the samples were filtered 
through a PP membrane syringe filter (0.22 μm) before analysis. The 
biomass samples (suspended sludges/biofilm) were freeze dried and 
ground to powder to enable extraction of the targeted compounds. The 
resulting powder weighed approximately 0.2–0.5 g before being trans­
ferred to a centrifuge tube, into which, 10 mL of 50 % methanol was 
added. The solvents were vortexed for a while and sonicated at 40 ◦C for 
15 min. Subsequently, the solvents were centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 
min, and the supernatants were collected in the beakers. The extracted 
sludges were repeatedly mixed with 10 mL of 50 % methanol and 
extracted by the same mentioned procedures, and the supernatants were 
collected in the same beakers for each sample. All of the supernatants 
were then extracted by the same SPE protocol with liquid samples. 
To analyze the targeted pharmaceuticals, an ultra-high-performance 
liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/ 
MS), Q Exactive™ Focus MS, UltiMate™ 3000 RSLC System (Thermo 
Scientific, USA) equipped with Orbitrap high resolution, and a heated 
electrospray ionization source (H-ESI II) was conducted for analysis of 
targeted compounds. For the mobile phase, 0.1 % formic acid in Milli-Q 
water (solvent A) and 0.1 % formic acid in methanol (solvent B) were 
used. The gradient elution program with a flowrate of 0.2 mL/min was 
initiated with 20 % solvent B for 1 min with the solvent concentration 
then increased linearly to 90 % over 4 min. The solvent concentration 
was then held at 90 % for 2 min, before being reduced to 20 % for 3 min 
to equilibrate. A Thermo Hypersil GOLD™ C18 column (150 mm × 2.1 
mm, 5 μm particle size, 175 Å pore size) was used at a constant tem­
perature of 40 ◦C. The injection volume was 5 μL. The polarity was 
operated in the positive mode of ESI for MS parameters. The HESI source 
parameters consisted of an Aux gas heater temperature of 300 ◦C, 
capillary temperature of 250 ◦C, S-len RF level of 50 and spray voltage of 
2.8 kV. Ultrapure nitrogen was employed both as the source gas for ions 
and as the gas used for collisions. It was utilized in the following pro­
portions: 40 au for sheath gas, 10 au for auxiliary gas, and 2 au for sweep 
gas. The Orbitrap was operated in parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) 
mode with 35,000 resolution targeted-MS2. The mass range in the PRM 
was scanned at 50.0–280.0 m/z. Maximum injection time was auto­
mated, and the automatic gain control (AGC) target in the PRM was 
established at a value of 5 × 104 ions. Normalized collision energy (NCE) 
was stepped at 20 and 30 V for PRM, while an isolation window was set 
at 3.0 m/z. The acquisition state for instrument control was operated in 
Xcalibur, and TraceFinder was used for processing the data. The SPE 
recovery was validated by the differences of the peak areas of the target 
compounds in the mixed standards before SPE (solution A) and after SPE 
(solutions B): R (%) = (A/B) × 100. The SPE recovery of the SMX was 
80.55 %, while for the other compounds, it was 100 %. The limit of 
detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ) were calculated as the 
standard concentrations in line with signal to noise ratios (S/N) of 3:1 
and 10:1, respectively. The LC-MS/MS Orbitrap data are provided in 
Supplementary Data Table S2 and Fig. S6. The standard calibration 
curves of each compound are provided at 0.5–25 μg/L and 50–1000 μg/L 
with a high level of accuracy (R2 > 0.99). 
2.5. Mass balance analysis of targeted pharmaceuticals 
The mass balance of the targeted pharmaceuticals in each C3, which 
refers to different redox conditions in each bioreactor, was calculated, 
taking into account the removal mechanisms of biodegradation, sorp­
tion in the biomass (suspended sludge/biofilm) and wasted sludges 
using Eq. (2): 
Minf = MS,MVB + MS,MLSS−C3 + Mb,C3 + Meff + Mwasted sludge
(2)  
where Minf and Meff are pharmaceutical loads in the influent and effluent 
through the experimental run (μg), respectively, MS,MVB and MS,MLSS-C3 
are pharmaceuticals removed by adsorption in biofilm on MVB and 
MLSS, respectively (μg), Mb,C3 is amounts of pharmaceutical removed by 
biodegradation in compartment 3 (μg) and Mwasted sludge is pharmaceu­
tical load of wasted sludge from compartment 3 through the experi­
mental run (μg). 
Regarding the calculation for sorption by the biofilm on MVB, 
sorption by MLSS in C3, and sorption in the wasted sludges, Eqs. (3), (4)

2.6. Batch test for degradation kinetics and adsorption isotherm 
Batch biotransformation experiments were performed to observe and 
compare the kinetic degradation of the targeted pharmaceuticals under 
anaerobic and microaerobic conditions. High-rise building wastewater 
was used in the batch test, and it was spiked with the targeted phar­
maceuticals in various concentrations in 500 mL beakers placed on a 
magnetic stirrer plate to ensure proper mixing. The MVBs (biofilms) in 
C3 from R1 (for the anaerobic batch test) and R2 (for the microaerobic 
batch test) were filled into the beaker at 30 % by volume, and the sus­
pended sludges in C3 from each bioreactor were washed with Milli-Q 
water, centrifuged for 5 min, and diluted until the corresponding bea­
kers contained 300 mg MLSS/L. Four concentration levels ranging from 
ten to thousands μg/L were used for this test. The methanol added from 
the spiking in highest concentration contributed to COD of approxi­
mately 700 mg/L in the batch system. To ensure the COD was consistent

3.1. Effect of microaeration and sludge recirculation on biomass 
characteristics, VFAs and dissolved methane removal 
Fig. 2(a) shows the ratio and the biomass concentrations of the 
biofilms on the MVBs and MLSS in C3 of the three bioreactors. It was 
found that the average biomass concentrations were significantly 
increased in the microaerobic AnBB-MBRs (R2 and R3) in both biofilms 
and MLSS as compared to R1: AnBB-MBR. The ratios of the biofilm/ 
MLSS were reduced from 0.92 in R1 to 0.82 in R2, which indicates that 
microaeration played a vital role in the enhancement of suspended 
biomass growth rather than biofilm formation. However, the decline in 
MLSS of C3 in R3 as compared to R2 might be from the sludge recir­
culation to the entrapment of MLSS within a fixed film. In the presence 
of oxygen, microorganisms degrade organics and nutrients as the growth 
substrates which can provide higher growth yields (biofilm and sus­
pended biomass) than in anaerobic conditions (Thoai et al., 2023). In 
addition, a small amount of oxygen 0.93 LO2/Lfeed could help increase 
the microorganism activities, promoting the formation of biomass, 
resulting in a broader and larger range of particle size distribution (Fig. 2 
(b)) compared to the sole anaerobic process. The particle size distribu­
tion in the R2 and R3 were in the range of 2 to 586 μm and 2 to 400 μm,

regardless of the reactor configurations or redox environment. CAF is 
hydrophilic molecules and contains the methyl group (-CH3), which is 
an electron donating group that can be easily degraded by demethyla­

oxidation from aerobes (Gummadi et al., 2012). For SMX, previous 
studies have consistently found that it was removed by biodegradation, 
while low adsorption was observed in various redox conditions the 
results of this study (aerobic, anaerobic, anoxic/aerobic) and waste­
water treatment technologies (Alvarino et al., 2016; Alvarino et al., 
2014; Iliopoulou et al., 2023; Wijekoon et al., 2015). In line with this 
study, biodegradation is the major pathway for the removal of SMX, and 
it has been found that the use of microaeration (0.93 LO2/Lfeed) and 
microaeration with sludge recirculation can enhance the biodegradation 
efficiency. The presence of electron-donating groups, amine group 
(−NH2) and -CH3, in SMX structures might promote its biodegradation 
in oxygen availability. Stadler et al. (2015) also found that 62 % of SMX 
was biodegraded in the microaerobic process and by over 35 % and 38 % 
in anoxic/aerobic and aerobic sequencing batch reactors, respectively. 
The reductive biotransformation of SMX under less negative redox po­

cleavage of the sulfonyl group and isoxazole ring (Alvarino et al., 2018).

C3 of R2, >5 % in C3 of R3, and no removal observed in C3 of R1. DCF, 
an aromatic amine, exhibits the propensity to generate nitro derivatives 
in the presence of nitrites, and these derivatives tend to revert to the 
original compound upon the reduction of nitrites in an anaerobic envi­
ronment (Iliopoulou et al., 2023). The removal pathways of DCF fol­
lowed the same trends as observed in previous comparative studies of 
the aerobic and anaerobic process degradation of DCF, which shows its 
low biodegradability and insignificant difference in removal outcomes 
under these redox conditions (Alvarino et al., 2018; Alvarino et al., 
2014; Iliopoulou et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2020). The presence of the 
chloro group (–Cl), which is an electron withdrawing group might 
render diclofenac recalcitrant for biodegradation processes. Dechlori­
nation was reported as the main mechanism in the removal of DCF under 
anaerobic reductive condition by using chlorine as the final electron 
acceptors by anaerobic microbes (Yang et al., 2022). Moreover, Poirier- 
Larabie et al. (2016) stated that oxygen played a vital role in the hy­
droxylation of the phenyl of DCF.

Table 2 shows the kbio values of the targeted pharmaceuticals at 
various concentrations in the microaerobic and anaerobic batch degra­
dation tests. The biotransformation kinetics under both conditions could 
fit to pseudo-first order kinetics with R2 ranging from 0.77 to 0.99. The 
kbio of CIP increased as the CIP concentration increased under micro­
aerobic condition from 0.008 h−1 to 0.020 h−1, and CIP did not inhibit 
the microaerobic microbial activity at the highest concentration 
(6801.92 μg/L), whereas the anaerobic biomass kept kbio quite constant 
at 0.004–0.008 h−1. In this study, it was observed that the ciprofloxacin 
in the building wastewater tended to undergo adsorption onto sludge 
rather than biodegradation in the presence of oxygen. This can explain 
why no inhibition of CIP was observed under microaerobic conditions at 
the highest concentration. Owing to the occurrence of both biodegra­
dation and adsorption in the batch test, the higher kbio values of CIP 
under microaerobic conditions than those under anaerobic conditions in 
all concentrations is partly due to the greater adsorption capacity by 
electrostatic interaction and cation bridging of the microaerobic 
biomass as described in Section 3.2. CAF is well known to be a highly 
biodegraded compound, regardless of redox conditions (aerobic, anoxic, 
and anaerobic) (de Wilt et al., 2018) providing the highest kbio of 0.044 
h−1 at the CAF concentration of 177.8 μg/L under microaerobic 
conditions. 
This study also found that the kbio values of SMX at relevant con­
centration in the environment at 28.55–291.46 μg/L were higher under 
microaerobic conditions (0.019–0.040 h−1) than those under anaerobic 
conditions (0.005–0.009 h−1). Likewise regarding the results for the 
removal and fate of SMX in Fig. 5(b), most previous research has found 
that SMX was more efficiently biotransformed in soils and sludges under 
the presence of oxygen with higher kbio values than in an absence of 
oxygen (Biel-Maeso et al., 2019; Lakshminarasimman et al., 2018; Liu 
et al., 2010). For DCF, the relevant kbio values and higher concentrations 
in the AnBB-MBR system (67.24–2314.15 μg/L) tended to be higher 
under microaerobic conditions than under anaerobic conditions. 
Alvarino et al. (2014) proposed a kbio of DCF in activated sludge of 0.1 L/ 
g.MLSS-d, which was higher than that in UASB at 0.007 L/g.MLSS-d, 
which concurs with the findings of this study. However, Iliopoulou et al. 
(2023) found that no kbio values of DCF were observed in batch tests 
carried out in both anaerobic and aerobic MBRs due to its refractory 
biotransformation. In summary, the overall results with this developed 
AnBB-MBR system show that most of the target compounds were 
removed in greater amounts under microaerobic conditions than 
anaerobic conditions corresponding to the continuous operation of 
AnBB-MBRs. 
In order to eliminate the effects of biodegradation, the inactivated 
biomasses were used to study the adsorption isotherms of the targeted 
compounds. It was found that the adsorption isotherms of the targeted 
pharmaceuticals under microaerobic and anaerobic conditions could be 
better fitted with the Freundlich model than the Langmuir model in the 
range of the test concentrations of all compounds (R2 > 0.9). The fitted 
results of the Freundlich model are shown in Fig. 7 and Supplementary 
Data Table S4. The biomass surface heterogeneity and multilayer 
adsorption are Freundlich model which used Kf to indicate the affinity of 
compound to biomass or biosorption capacity and 1/n to indicate 
adsorbed surface heterogeneity with high adsorption intensity when the 
1/n values is nearly zero (Cao et al., 2019). Due to the naturally negative 
charges of biomass, the positively charged compounds tended to be 
adsorbed by electrostatic interaction much more effectively than by 
neutral compounds and negative substances, respectively (Kahle and 
Stamm, 2007). 
Freundlich isotherms show that microaerobic biomass could improve 
CIP adsorption onto the biomass as compared to anaerobic biomass, 
with microaerobic biomass and anaerobic biomass having Kf and 1/n 
values of 6.50 L/g and 0.42, and 1.72 L/g and 0.57, respectively. CIP has 
the lowest 1/n values as compared to the other compounds, which in­
dicates that CIP was strongly adsorbed onto the biomass, and the Kf 
values were in line with previous research of CIP adsorption onto acti­
vated sludges and aerobic granular sludges (Ferreira et al., 2016). This 
result is in accordance with the reasons for the adsorption of CIP as 
earlier discussed in Section 3.2, whereby microaerobic biomass tended 
to adsorb CIP to a greater degree than anaerobic biomass did. For CAF 
and SMX, the differences in the adsorption isotherms between the 
microaerobic and the anaerobic biomass were found to be insignificant. 
CAF exists in a cationic form, while SMX and DCF are anionic com­
pounds in neutral pH (pH around 7), which led to higher sorption of CAF 
onto negative sludges than those of two compounds and in accordance 
with their Kd values (Table S2). SMX and DCF were less absorbed onto 
the negatively charged biomass with Kf in the range of 0.01–0.12 L/g.

contributing factor that could enhance the removal efficiency of the 
targeted compounds when microaeration at 0.93 LO2/Lfeed is employed

0.80–1.20 % in the anaerobic biomass and at 0.10 % in the microaerobic

and SMX (Fan et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2019). This might lead to 
biodegradation becoming the primary process in the degradation of CIP 
and SMX under anaerobic conditions. Moreover, Leptolinea and Long­
ilinea, which are both members of the Anaerolineaceae family of strictly 
anaerobic filamentous bacteria, have the potential to produce the oxy­
genase enzymes, which could have participated in the cometabolism of 
the pharmaceuticals investigated in the present study. 
The anaerobic filamentous microorganisms, which consist of the 
genus of Pelolinea (0.58–0.68 %), Caldisericum (6.69–13.52 %), Long­
ilinea (1.14–1.61) and Leptolinea (3.94–3.69 %) were found in the

aerobic biomass (R2) and found at only low levels in R3 biomass for 
Longilinea (0.23–0.49 %) and Leptolinea (0.11–0.50 %). This is in 
accordance with SEM images, which show that anaerobic filamentous 
bacteria were enriched on the MVB biofilms of R1 and R3. These mi­

inducing significant levels of L-EPS (Fig. 6(b) and (c)), which exhibited 
high hydrophobicity, formed irregular flocs, and had a low zeta poten­

filtration within the anaerobic MBR system (Meng et al., 2006), which is 
consistent with results from the AnBB-MBR (R1) in this study. Even with 
the existence of these microorganisms in R3, there was still sludge 
recirculation that could alleviate membrane fouling by inducing shear 
force on to the foulants by the moving MVB. In addition, Desulfobrio, 
found at 0.15–1.50 % in the anaerobic biomass and not found in the 
microaerobic biomass, likely influenced the accumulation of organic 
fouling materials (Yao et al., 2021), thereby affecting the dynamics of 
the biocakes of R1. For other microbial groups, JG30-KF-CM45 are 
significant contributors to the breakdown of complex organic molecules 
in wastewater treatment plants (Huang et al., 2022). As these groups are 
more prevalent in the microaerobic biomass compared to the anaerobic 
biomass of R1, they might be crucial contributors to the removal of 
complex organic substances and foulants from the inlet building 
wastewater. Also, Pir4_lineage is associated with the microaerobic mi­
crobes that have been detected in anoxic or micro-oxic habitats (Dedysh 
et al., 2020). 
4. Conclusion 
The proposed AnBB-MBR with microaeration (R2) and AnBB-MBR 
with microaeration and sludge recirculation (R3) were employed in 
AnBB-MBR (R1) to enhance the removal of CIP, CAF, SMX and DCF from 
building wastewater. R2 and R3 showed notable enhancements in the 
removal of COD, VFAs, and dissolved methane, as well as in the 
reduction of the membrane fouling rate when compared to R1. C1 in the 
AnBB-MBRs were most responsible for the removal of all the targeted 
compounds. The highest removal of CIP (78.0 %) and DCF (40.8 %) 
occurred in R2, while the highest removal of SMX was in R3 at 91.3 %; 
whereas CAF was efficiently removed (>90 %) in all of the AnBB-MBR 
systems. Microaeration enhanced the adsorption of CIP onto the 
biomass and assisted the biodegradability of CAF, SMX and DCF in the 
AnBB-MBR, which were insisted by batch biotransformation kinetics 
and adsorption tests. Microaeration was found to be able to enrich the 
microbial groups that were responsible for the degradation of the tar­
geted pharmaceuticals. Overall, the proposed AnBB-MBR with microa­
eration is a promising solution for the treatment of building wastewater 
contaminated with pharmaceuticals.
